Cost and pricing
How much does a website cost? An honest anatomy of the price
Send the same brief to two studios. One says five million. The other says fifty million. Here is the odd part: both of them can be telling the truth.
21 November 2026·8 min read·Roxana and Arshia

In this article

  1. What does your money actually buy?
  2. How can five million and fifty million both be honest?
  3. Where a cheap quote quietly cuts
  4. What pushes the price around
  5. Seven questions to put to every quote
  6. Lists, not numbers

Summary

  1. A website price is hours of work, multiplied by how deeply each stage gets done. So do not compare the final number. Compare the list of work behind it.
  2. A cheap quote usually cuts the same three things: the written scope, testing a real payment, and handover with documents. You pay for all three later, and it costs more then.
  3. A quote that will not write down what is NOT included is hiding the priciest part of any project: the surprises.

Someone asks us this almost every week: that place quoted five million, why is yours this much? The short answer is that “a website” is not one product. It is a chain of jobs, and every quote picks a different stretch of that chain. Until you can see the list of work, comparing two numbers is comparing two sealed boxes.

So here is what usually only gets said inside a sales meeting, published instead: what your money buys, hour by hour, which parts can be cut, and who ends up paying for the cut, and when. Read it, then go and get quotes. From us, from anyone.
What does your money actually buy?
A website price is built from seven stages. In any quote you are handed, each stage is done properly, done thinly, or simply not there. And its absence never shows in the final number:

rows: Conversation and scope
The goal, the pages and the features get fixed on paper, and signed
Every vagueness left here costs several times more once the project is underway
Structure and page map
The order of the pages, and the path a customer walks from landing to paying, get laid out
Guess this wrong and it is a redesign in the middle of the job
Interface design
Pages designed in your brand’s look, with rounds of review
Every review round is a full round of designing and checking
Build and development
The design becomes a working site: shop, gateway, forms, admin panel
A feature is one line on paper. In real life it is detail and edge cases all the way down
Content entry
Your real words and photos replace the placeholders, and get arranged properly
Content that is not ready is the most common reason launch day slides
Testing
A real purchase with a real card, on phones and browsers, forms and error paths all tried for real
A bug your customer finds first costs several times the test. You pay it in lost sales
Handover and training
Access, the maintenance documents and admin training actually reach you
Without this, every tiny change keeps you dependent on whoever built it

blocks.html: From now on, when someone gives you a number, ask one question: which rows of this table are in it, how deeply, and which rows are missing altogether? That answer explains about ninety percent of the difference between prices.
How can five million and fifty million both be honest?

Because the two of you are usually talking about two different things. One quote might be a five page brochure site, built on a ready template, with content you supply yourself. The other might be a full shop: payment gateway, order SMS, invoicing, a connection to your accounting, design made from scratch. Both get called “a website”. One is a bicycle, the other is a van. Of course the prices differ.

The depth differs too. In one shop, testing means opening the site in one browser to check it loads. In another it means paying with a real card, watching a payment fail, coming back from the bank, and trying the whole thing on three phones, cheap ones and expensive ones. Both call it testing. One takes two hours. The other takes two days.

And the people differ. A freelancer carries no office and no team, so they finish cheaper, but their capacity and their support are one person deep. A studio costs more because the roles are separate, and if one person gets sick the project does not fall asleep. None of that is fraud. What matters is knowing which one you are actually buying. The most dangerous sentence in this market is “a complete website, only this much”, because complete means nothing until there is a list to measure it against.
Most of the gap between two prices is not the builder’s profit. It is the work that was quietly taken out.
Where a cheap quote quietly cuts
When a number sits far below everyone else, the discount does not come out of the builder’s profit. It comes out of your work. Learn the three places it usually gets cut:

items: The scope: no written list gets signed, which is exactly how the price stays low. Then every “just add one page” and “I thought payment was included” turns into an argument, and a separate charge. You start cheap and pay the rest in instalments, in nerves.

The testing: the gateway gets connected, sure. But a failed purchase, backing out at the bank page, an SMS that never arrives: never tried. Your first real tester becomes your first real customer, and the fee is lost sales and dented trust.

The handover: domain and hosting stay in the builder’s name, no training happens, no documents arrive. Changing one phone number means a phone call, and a wait. That dependence is the hidden instalment plan of a cheap website, and it has no ceiling on it.

blocks.html: To be clear: cheap is not automatically bad. If your job is small and you take these three cuts with your eyes open, your choice can be the right one. The bad version is the hidden cut, where you believe you bought something and only find out on delivery day that you did not.
What pushes the price around
Want a better guess before you start collecting quotes? These are the main levers on website cost:

items: How many pages there are, what kind, and how many need a design of their own.
Whether there is a shop and a payment gateway, or the site only introduces you.
Whether words and photos are ready, or somebody has to make and arrange them.
Whether it is one language or two.
Connections to other systems: SMS, accounting, stock, booking.
Templated design, partly custom, or fully custom.
How much of a rush you are in. Squashed, deadline driven work almost always costs more.

blocks.html: This is why we do not hang a fixed price on our site, and why the scope comes first. A number with no list behind it is just a number. We published our whole scope template in the project scope article, so you can carry the same sheet of paper to anyone and compare quotes fairly.
Seven questions to put to every quote
Put these seven questions to every builder, and ask for the answers in writing. A quote that answers them on paper, even a pricier one, tends to end up cheaper in real life:

items: Where, in the document, is the list of pages and features, line by line?
What is explicitly NOT included in this price?
Does the price include testing a real purchase with a real card?
Whose name are the domain and hosting in, and who holds the full access?
What training, and what documents, come with the handover?
How many review rounds are included, and what does extra work cost?
After handover, if something breaks, how long is it supported, and how?

blocks.html: If the answer to any of them is “we will see how it goes”, you have just found the spot where the real price starts parting company with the number on the paper.
Lists, not numbers

You cannot squeeze a website’s cost into one honest number, but you can make it transparent: seven stages, with the depth and the cuts out in the open. Lists, not numbers. And when a number sounds too good, do not hunt for the discount. Hunt for the deleted row of the table. It is almost always there.
Now run your own project through it
Our project estimator works off these same levers: pick the features, get a brief and a rough range back. The final number, as ever, gets set by the written scope. Not by a web form.
